summary: This document describes threats to location information, especially for emergency calls, and techniques that improve its reliability and security. It also offers guidelines for judging how trustworthy a location is.

eli5.summary: If you tell the fire department where you are, they must trust that it is true. This RFC explains how location claims can be faked and how to make them more believable.

questions: how can attackers fake emergency location
subtitle: How to verify location claims and prevent spoofing in emergency services.

tldr.problem: Attackers can spoof location information in emergency calls by claiming to be at a different location, replaying old location, or stealing location from others, making it hard for dispatchers to send help to the right place.
tldr.mechanism: Three techniques strengthen location trustworthiness: location servers sign location information so spoofing is detectable; location-by-reference lets emergency centers fetch location directly from the source; proxies intercept calls and add verified location based on network access.
tldr.outcome: When location information is signed, referenced from a trusted server, or added by a network intermediary, emergency dispatchers can assess how much to trust it and dispatch help more reliably.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Informational; focuses on malicious end host model

facts.label: Primary use case
facts.value: Emergency calling and IP-based emergency services

facts.label: Location representation
facts.value: PIDF-LO (Presence Information Data Format Location Object)

today: RFC 7378 is an informational document describing the landscape of location spoofing threats and mitigation techniques. The three approaches it describes are variously deployed or under development in emergency services networks worldwide, with location-by-reference seeing increasing adoption for its security properties.

sections.title: Location in Emergency Calling
sections.content:
Location information is critical for emergency services. When someone calls 911 or a local emergency number, the Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) must determine the caller's location to dispatch appropriate response. For traditional landline calls, location is determined from a database lookup of the phone number. For IP-based emergency services from mobile or nomadic devices, the device itself may provide location information within the emergency call.

IP-based emergency services introduce new threats. A malicious caller can fabricate location information in the call signaling, deceiving the PSAP into dispatching help to the wrong location. Identity spoofing compounds the problem: if a caller can spoof their phone number or identity, the PSAP cannot even rely on location history to verify the claim. Hoax calls—both false emergencies and those with false locations—divert resources from people in real danger.
sections.eli5: Emergency calls need to reach the right place. With old phones, the phone number told you where someone was. With cell phones and internet calls, the person can lie about their location.

sections.title: How Location Can Be Faked
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three main location spoofing attacks. Place shifting occurs when an attacker constructs location information claiming to be at an arbitrary location, possibly outside their actual cell coverage. Time shifting happens when an attacker reuses old location information from when they were somewhere else, exploiting the fact that signatures have validity windows. Location theft occurs when an attacker captures another person's location information (possibly including a cryptographic signature) and presents it as their own.

The document also distinguishes three adversary models. In the external adversary model, the attacker is outside the emergency system infrastructure, between the end host and the location server or PSAP. In the malicious infrastructure model, location servers or call routing infrastructure itself is compromised. In the malicious end host model, the device initiating the call acts maliciously. The RFC focuses on the malicious end host scenario, where the calling device itself provides false location.
sections.eli5: An attacker can pretend to be somewhere they are not. They can use location that was true yesterday but is false today. They can steal someone else's location proof and use it. The system must catch these tricks.

sections.title: Three Ways to Prevent Location Spoofing
sections.content:
The RFC describes three mitigation techniques. Signed location-by-value has the location server digitally sign the location information before sending it to the device. The device conveys the signed location in the emergency call, and the PSAP verifies the signature. However, this approach has limitations: without an identity element in the signature, an attacker can still cut-and-paste location from another device; the signature includes a validity window (an "until" timestamp), requiring periodic refresh even for stationary users; and signed location cannot stop denial-of-service attacks where an attacker launches many emergency calls with valid signed locations.

Location-by-reference avoids these problems by having the location server issue a reference (a URI) instead of location-by-value. The device sends only the reference in the emergency call. The PSAP then fetches actual location directly from the location server over a protected channel, ensuring the location is fresh and cannot be modified by intermediaries. References expire after a time to prevent indefinite tracking. Proxy-added location takes a different approach: network proxies operated by ISPs intercept SIP emergency calls and add location information based on the caller's IP address or network access identity, replacing or supplementing any location the end device provided.
sections.eli5: One way: the location server signs the location like a notary stamps a document so you know it is real. Another way: instead of sending location, send a receipt and let the emergency center ask the location server for the real location. A third way: a network box intercepts the call and adds real location based on what network the caller is on.

sections.title: Assessing Trustworthiness
sections.content:
The RFC defines trustworthy location as location information that can be attributed to a trusted source, has been protected against modification in transit, and has been assessed as trustworthy. Location trust assessment is the process of evaluating how reliable location information is.

A PSAP call taker should be able to assess in real time the level of trust to place in conveyed location. If location is unsigned and came directly from the caller's device, trust should be low. If location is signed by a reputable location information server (LIS), trust is higher. If location was fetched by the PSAP directly from the LIS over a secure channel, trust is highest. If location came from a proxy-added mechanism based on network access identity, trust depends on the strength of that network authentication and the trustworthiness of the proxy.

Where real-time assessment is impossible, post-incident investigations must be able to determine the source of a call for accountability. This requires logging mechanisms and the ability to trace location claims back to their origin.
sections.eli5: A dispatcher needs to ask: Did this location come from the person calling (not trustworthy), from a trusted location service (more trustworthy), or from the network itself (most trustworthy)? The answer determines how much to rely on the location.

sections.title: Building a Trustworthy System
sections.content:
Implementing trustworthy location requires careful architecture. For signed location-by-value, location information servers must be rooted in a trusted Certificate Authority. The RFC notes that certificates for location services should be issued with clear governance, possibly through a hierarchy rooted in a Valid Emergency Services Authority. Validity windows on signatures must be calibrated: too short requires frequent refreshes, too long allows time-shifting attacks.

For location-by-reference, location information servers must maintain multiple URIs per target with expiration times to prevent tracking and enable garbage collection. PSAP systems must authenticate to location servers (possibly via client certificates) to dereference URIs securely. Dereferencing must use TLS to protect both the location data and the URL itself from eavesdropping.

For proxy-added location, ISPs must deploy application-layer proxies at network edge points, requiring coordination between Internet Access Providers and Voice Service Providers, who may lack business relationships. The proxy becomes fully responsible for the accuracy and timeliness of location it adds.
sections.eli5: For signatures to work, there needs to be a trusted authority issuing certificates to location servers. For reference-based methods, location servers need security and expiration policies. For proxies to work, ISPs need the right equipment in the right places.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that location information is sensitive. Privacy must be preserved; PIDF-LO objects are designed to limit identifying information to protect targets, using unlinked pseudonyms rather than device identifiers when possible. However, emergency services may disable privacy protections to enable real-time attribution.

Security mechanisms must prevent attacks on emergency service infrastructure itself. Solutions must defend against denial-of-service attacks launched through emergency calls, such as attackers initiating many calls with different spoofed locations to overwhelm the system. Authentication mechanisms must account for the time-critical nature of emergency calls; multi-layer authentication that delays response is unacceptable. Accountability mechanisms should enable law enforcement to identify hoax callers after the fact, providing a deterrent through the threat of prosecution.
sections.eli5: Location is private information. Emergency calls should not leak location to unnecessary parties. Bad people might try to overwhelm emergency centers with fake calls. The system must work fast and allow police to investigate false alarms afterward.
